meaning: Possibly from πηγή (spring) or a pre-Greek name

pronunciation.approximation: PAY-ga-sos, with the stacked macron+acute on the first ē.
pronunciation.note: Pḗgasos bears a name that is probably not Greek at all: scholars connect it to the Luwian storm god pihassas, carried into Greek myth through Anatolian contact. The folk etymology from πηγή, "spring," was already popular in antiquity — the horse who stamps springs from the rock. Attic inscriptions spell the name with the long ē of the first syllable — the quantity the restoration keeps.

domains.title: The Thunder-Horse
domains.subtitle: Springs, Lightning, and the Flight to Olympos
domains.lead: Pḗgasos springs from the severed neck of Médousa at the moment of her death — beauty erupting from horror — and ends as the thunder-bearer of Zeús and a constellation. He is the only winged horse of Greek myth with a name, and his route runs from blood to stars.

cards.name: The Wings
cards.desc: From sea-foam blood to the sky — the emblem of unbounded ascent.

cards.name: Hippocrene
cards.desc: The Horse's Spring on Mount Helikṓn, struck open by his hoof — the poets' fountain of inspiration.

cards.name: The Chimaira
cards.desc: Bellerophōn's fire-breathing foe, fought from the saddle of the flying horse.

cards.name: Bearer of Thunder
cards.desc: Hesiod gives him Olympus's strangest job: carrying Zeús' thunder and lightning.

symbols.name: The golden bridle
symbols.meaning: Athēnā's gift to Bellerophōn — divine technique mastering divine power

symbols.name: The hoof-print
symbols.meaning: The spring-maker; inspiration struck from stone

symbols.name: The constellation
symbols.meaning: His final shape — the great square of Pegasus riding the autumn sky

mythology.lead: Pḗgasos is the bridge-figure of Greek myth: born in a monster story, ridden in a hero story, employed in a god story — three genres, one horse.

myths.title: Out of the Gorgon
myths.text: Hesiod tells it in four lines: when Perseus cut the head from Médousa, out sprang great Pḗgasos and the warrior Chrysaōr — her children by Poseidṓn. The horse flew to the "immortal ones," and Hesiod already knows his office: "he lives in the halls of Zeús, carrying thunder and lightning for the counsellor."

myths.title: Bellerophōn's Gift
myths.text: The hero Bellerophōn, sent to Lykia with a letter demanding his own death, was ordered to kill the Chimaira. Píndar sings how Athēnā appeared with a golden bridle — "take this charm for the horse" — and how, sacrificing to Poseidṓn the horse-breaker, Bellerophōn caught Pḗgasos at the spring of Peirene and from the air slew the fire-breathing beast.

myths.title: The Flight Too High
myths.text: Success bred the fatal wish: Bellerophōn tried to fly to Olympos itself. Zeús sent a gadfly to sting the horse, and the rider fell back to earth to wander the Aleian plain alone — Pindar's model of hybris punished — while Pḗgasos continued upward to the stables of the gods.

myths.title: The Fountain of the Horse
myths.text: On Helikṓn, mountain of the Muses, Pḗgasos struck the rock with his hoof and opened Hippocrene, the Horse's Spring, whose water makes poets. The image outlasted the cult: every later trope of inspiration — the struck rock, the flying horse, the intoxicating water — is his hoofprint.

lore.syncretism: His name is the syncretism: Luwian pihassas, a storm-god honoured in Cilicia, meets the Greek horse — which explains why an earth-and-sea creature serves the sky god's bolts. Rome made him a cavalry emblem and a favourite of coinage; Corinth stamped him on her silver for three centuries as the city's own beast, since Bellerophōn's Corinthian Peirene was his watering place.
lore.culturalLegacy: Pḗgasos became the western shorthand for poetic flight — from the Renaissance "hobby-horse of the Muses" to Pope's mock-epic. His silhouette is arguably the most commercially licensed image from Greek myth: the red Pegasus of Mobil Oil flew over filling stations across the planet, and the TriStar Pictures logo opens thousands of films. Astronomy keeps his body nightly; literature keeps his spring.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Pḗgasos proves that origin is not destiny. Born of blood and salt and horror, he ends as pure ascent — the horse of storms who chooses the sky. He is the emblem of every act of imagination that takes off from wreckage: the spring in the stone, the poem in the wound.

And he remains the honest emblem of inspiration because the myth hides none of it: the gift is caught, not earned — a bridle in a dream, a spring in a stone — and it throws the rider who mistakes it for his own wings. Every artist who has flown on something they did not make, and every one who has been dropped for flying too high on it, knows exactly whose back they were on.
lore.archaeology: Corinthian coinage is the standing archive: silver staters showing Pḗgasos in flight, with the koppa letter of Corinth, survive in thousands from ca. 550–250 BCE. Vase painters loved the birth scene — Perseus recoiling as the foal springs out — and the Amphiaraos krater shows the full cast. Corinth's Peirene fountain-house, repeatedly rebuilt from Archaic to Roman times, is the physical site of the bridle myth.
